trap.10: You may have counted a jump rather than substituting n = 4.
trap.12: Check two times four, then add three.
trap.14: Recheck which column you are filling.
trap.16: Sixteen is one of the choices, but it is not this term.
trap.2n: Two n has the right difference, but it misses the plus three.
trap.3n+2: Look at the jump from five to seven. It is plus two, not plus three.

tasks.title: 02 · The adjustment can be negative
tasks.hint: The terms rise by three, but the first term is one. Try 3n minus 2.

trap.7: Seven is the third term. Use position four.
trap.12: Remember to subtract two after multiplying.
trap.15: Three times five is fifteen; subtract the adjustment.
trap.16: You have added rather than subtracted the adjustment.
trap.3n+2: The adjustment is minus two, not plus two.
trap.2n−3: The coefficient must match the +3 difference.

tasks.title: 03 · Work with a larger difference
tasks.hint: The terms increase by four. What must be added to 4n to produce five at n = 1?

trap.16: Four times four is sixteen. What is the adjustment?
trap.20: Four times five is twenty. Add one.
trap.25: This is not the next term from twenty-one.
trap.4n: The difference four is right, but the extra one is missing.
trap.n+4: The coefficient is not one: each term increases by four.

data.narration: The next term is found by multiplying by the same factor each time. For doubling, term n is two times two to the power n minus one.
data.prompt: Explain why a fixed multiplier is not the same as a fixed difference.

steps.name: see-the-first-term
steps.narration: Start with two. That is term one, not the amount we add each time.
steps.prompt: Read the first value. What could make it grow?

steps.name: multiply-once
steps.narration: Multiply two by two to reach four. The bar doubles.
steps.prompt: Why does multiplication give the next bar?

steps.name: multiply-again
steps.narration: Multiply by two again. Four becomes eight.
steps.prompt: What operation stays the same?

steps.name: keep-the-ratio
steps.narration: Every step doubles: two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two. The jumps get bigger, but the multiplier is unchanged.
steps.prompt: Do we add the same number each time?

steps.name: halving-contrast
steps.narration: Geometric sequences can shrink too. Sixty-four divided by two becomes thirty-two, then sixteen, then eight.
steps.prompt: How can you tell that each value is halved?

traps.58: Adding four does not continue the pattern.

STEPS.text: The first difference is three. Check the next jump too.
STEPS.prompt: Does adding three work twice in a row?

STEPS.name: test-a-false-rule
STEPS.text: If we doubled five, we would get ten, not eight. That rule fails.
STEPS.prompt: Why does multiply by two fail the very first step?

STEPS.name: the-matched-rule
STEPS.text: Add three works on every jump. Now the mystery rule is proven.
STEPS.prompt: Use the rule to predict the next term.

STEPS.name: a-reverse-mystery
STEPS.text: This mystery gets smaller by four each time. Every hop subtracts four.
STEPS.prompt: What is twenty minus four, then sixteen minus four?

STEPS.name: multiplying-instead
STEPS.text: Two, four, eight, sixteen. The amounts added change, but doubling works every time.
STEPS.prompt: Why is add two not the rule for the whole sequence?

TASKS.heading: 01 · Which rule always works?
TASKS.guide: Mystery sequence: 5, 8, 11, 14, 17. Choose the same operation for every jump.

trap.+4: Adding four to five gives nine, not eight. Try the first jump again.
trap.×2: Doubling five gives ten, not eight. Multiplying is not this rule.

TASKS.heading: 02 · A shrinking pattern
TASKS.guide: Mystery sequence: 24, 20, 16, 12, 8. Each term is smaller. Find the fixed change.

trap.+4: The terms are shrinking. Adding four would make them bigger.
trap.÷2: Half of twenty-four is twelve, not twenty. This is a fixed subtraction.

TASKS.heading: 03 · What makes it double?
TASKS.guide: Mystery sequence: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. The gaps change; the rule must not.

trap.+2: Two plus two gives four, but four plus two is six, not eight. The rule must work twice.
trap.×3: Two times three gives six, not four. Test the first jump.

sample: Five, eight, eleven. What might the hidden rule be?

TASKS.title: 01 · Finish the growing sequence
TASKS.guide: 4, 7, 10, __, __. Use the same add-three rule for both spaces.

trap.10: Ten is already the third term. Continue forward, not backwards.
trap.14: Fourteen is four more than ten. This rule adds three, not four.
trap.17: Seventeen is four more than thirteen. Check the hop size.

TASKS.title: 02 · Keep subtracting four
TASKS.guide: 24, 20, 16, __, __. Both missing terms must keep the same subtraction.

trap.4: Four is too many steps ahead. Continue one hop at a time.
trap.10: Sixteen subtract four gives twelve, not ten.
trap.20: Twenty already appears as term two. Continue downwards.

TASKS.title: 03 · Double to continue
TASKS.guide: 2, 4, 8, __, __. Check what happens to the multiplication rule each time.

trap.12: Eight plus four gives twelve, but the sequence doubles instead.
trap.18: Eighteen is not twice eight. Try multiplication by two.
trap.24: Twenty-four is eight more than sixteen. Doubling gives thirty-two.

steps.name: whole-triangle
steps.narration: We begin with one whole triangle. That is iteration zero.
steps.prompt: How many triangles can you see before anything changes?

steps.name: split-and-remove
steps.narration: Keep the three corner triangles. The middle triangle is removed.
steps.prompt: Count only the remaining corner triangles.

steps.name: repeat-the-rule
steps.narration: Repeat that same step for every triangle. Each one leaves three new triangles.
steps.prompt: How many remain after each of the three triangles is split?

steps.name: generalise-the-pattern
steps.narration: One, three, nine, twenty-seven. The number of triangles triples each time.
steps.prompt: Explain why the number is three to the power of the iteration.

steps.name: koch-four-for-one
steps.narration: Now watch a different fractal. Each straight section becomes four short sections.
steps.prompt: Count the four new sections in place of the original one.

steps.name: koch-repeat-length
steps.narration: Each of the four sections becomes four more. Four times four makes sixteen sections.
steps.prompt: If the first line was nine centimetres, explain why iteration two totals sixteen centimetres.

TASKS.title: 01 · Count the surviving triangles
TASKS.guide: After three Sierpiński iterations, how many of the smallest triangles remain?

traps.9: Nine is iteration two. Repeat the three-for-one rule once more.
traps.81: Eighty-one is iteration four. You have repeated the rule one step too far.

TASKS.title: 02 · Count the Koch sections
TASKS.guide: The Koch curve is at iteration two. How many short straight sections does it have?

traps.8: Eight assumes only two new sections per previous section. Each becomes four.
traps.12: Twelve treats the growth as adding a fixed number. Multiply by four each time.

TASKS.title: 03 · Find the total length
TASKS.guide: The original Koch line was 9 cm. After two iterations, what is its TOTAL length?

traps.9: The total length is not unchanged: each segment is replaced by four third-length pieces.
traps.36: Thirty-six multiplies the length by four without accounting for each new piece being one third as long.
